memoryText: But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Romans 5:8 slowly, several times, and try to say it from memory. Then read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is the center of the gospel in a single sentence.

“But God shows his love for us.” The verse begins with a contrast. The previous verses spoke of how rare it is for anyone to die for another. “But God.” His love is a different kind of love. The word “shows” means to demonstrate or prove. The cross is God’s own demonstration of his love.

“In that while we were still sinners.” Notice the timing. Not after we cleaned up, or when we decided to follow him. We were still sinners, still enemies, still without strength. God’s love does not wait for us to be lovable.

“Christ died for us.” Here is the proof. God did not simply declare love; he acted at great cost. Christ died, and he died “for us,” in our place and for our benefit.

This verse is not just history; it is the foundation for security. If God loved us when we were sinners, how much more will he keep us now that we are his children (5:9-10)? Our assurance does not rest on our record but on his demonstration.

When you doubt that God loves you, say this verse. The cross is the answer.
weekInReview: This week you saw what flows from justification. Romans 5 began with peace with God, access to grace, and hope that does not put us to shame, and then traced our story in two heads: Adam, through whom sin and death came, and Christ, through whom the free gift of righteousness and life comes. A doctrinal pause on union with Christ showed that believers have died and risen with him. Romans 6 answered the charge that grace encourages sin: we were slaves of sin and have become slaves of righteousness, and the wages of sin is death but the free gift of God is eternal life. Romans 7 gave the struggle with the law and the cry of the wretched man, answered by Jesus Christ our Lord. A second doctrinal pause considered sanctification, in which God works in us both to will and to work. Then Romans 8 opened with no condemnation and closed with the unbreakable love of God.
reflectionQuestions: Paul says God showed his love for us while we were still sinners. How does it change you to know that God’s love did not wait for you to improve?
Romans 5 says that in Adam all died and in Christ all who believe are made righteous. Where do you still try to live as if you were under Adam’s headship, relying on yourself?
Romans 8:1 says there is now no condemnation. Which voice do you hear most often, the voice of condemnation or the voice of the Spirit? What would it take to listen to the second?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for dying for you while you were still a sinner.
Ask him to silence the voice of condemnation.
